body.back: The business is treated as separate from its owner; private transactions of the owner are not recorded in the business books.
Only items that can be measured in monetary terms are recorded in the accounts.
Assets are recorded at the price originally paid for them, not their current market value.
The business is assumed to continue trading for the foreseeable future, so assets are not valued as if being sold off.
Every transaction has two effects on the accounts: a debit entry and an equal credit entry.
Profits and assets are not overstated and losses and liabilities are not understated; record potential losses but not unrealised profits.
Revenue is recognised when goods or services are provided (the sale is made), not when payment is received.
Expenses incurred in a period are matched with the revenue they helped to earn in the same period.
The same accounting methods are used from one period to the next so that results can be compared.
Insignificant items are not recorded separately or in detail; only items large enough to influence decisions are treated as important.
Machinery (asset) increases and cash (asset) decreases by the same amount; debit machinery, credit cash.
